Empirical Research Plan: The Long‐Run Impact of the Colonial Mining Mita in Peru
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
   • Method: Sharp geographic regression discontinuity design (GRD).  
   • Rationale: The mita boundary is a legally defined, historically exogenous line drawn in 1573. Indigenous settlements on either side were otherwise similar but experienced a discrete change in exposure to forced labor. Treating distance to the boundary as the running (forcing) variable allows us to compare districts infinitesimally close to, but on opposite sides of, the boundary. The GRD therefore isolates plausibly random institutional exposure while holding geography constant.  
   • Estimation: Local‐linear regressions with triangular kernel weighting, optimal bandwidth selection (Calonico-Cattaneo-Titiunik), and robustness to spatial autocorrelation (e.g., Conley or province clustering).  

2. Treatment and Control  
   • Treatment indicator D_i = 1 if district centroid lies weakly inside the historical mita catchment area; D_i = 0 otherwise.  
   • Control (counterfactual): Districts lying just outside the boundary (but within a chosen bandwidth h) that were not subject to the mita.  
   • Timing: Treatment occurred 1573-1812. Outcomes are measured in ENAHO surveys 2000-present. Because exposure is time‐invariant at the district level, cross‐sectional GRD suffices; panel RD (multiple ENAHO waves) increases precision but does not change identification.  

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
   a. Continuity: In the absence of mita, potential outcomes (household consumption, child height, public‐goods provision) vary smoothly with distance to the boundary, so any discontinuity at zero is attributable to treatment. Plausibility: Boundary was drawn for administrative distance‐to‐mine reasons, not based on differential economic potential.  
   b. No sorting/manipulation: District centroids today cannot manipulate their historical location relative to a 16th-century line. Modern migration could bias results only if it is a discontinuous function of distance; we can test population density continuity.  
   c. SUTVA/local interference: Outcomes in one district are not affected by treatment status of sufficiently distant districts; within-bandwidth spillovers are limited. Given rugged terrain and historically poor transport, local spillovers are plausible but likely decrease with distance—address via narrow bandwidth and robustness to donut RD.  
   d. Correct functional form: Using local linear fits within optimally chosen bandwidth and testing robustness to alternative bandwidths and higher-order polynomials mitigates bias.  
   e. Stable boundary: The mapped boundary is measured without error; we verify using historical cartography and modern GIS shapefiles.  

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
   1. Differential geography or pre-colonial characteristics right at the boundary.  
      • Mitigation: (i) show continuity in pre‐treatment covariates—Inka road proximity, pre‐1550 population density, elevation, slope, soil quality; (ii) include these controls flexibly; (iii) placebo RD on pre‐colonial outcomes.  
   2. Spatial correlation in errors leading to understated standard errors.  
      • Mitigation: Cluster at province level and implement Conley (1999) spatial HAC within 100-km cutoff; report both.  
   3. Modern infrastructure may have been deliberately routed differently inside vs. outside the mita, producing spatial general‐equilibrium effects beyond the local boundary.  
      • Mitigation: (i) Use narrow bandwidths (10–50 km) so major highways are often orthogonal; (ii) include distance to nearest main road or city as controls; (iii) run donut RD excluding districts intersected by national highways.  

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# 0. Packages --------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)             # spatial merges
library(rdrobust)        # RD estimation
library(rddensity)       # manipulation test
library(conleyreg)       # spatial HAC

# 1. Data ---------------------------------------------------------------
mita <- read_csv("district_mita_boundary.csv")      # district_id, inside_mita, dist_boundary_km
enaho <- read_csv("enaho_2000_2022.csv")           # survey data with outcomes
geo   <- read_csv("district_geography.csv")        # elevation, ruggedness, etc.

data <- enaho %>%
  left_join(mita, by = "district_id") %>%
  left_join(geo,  by = "district_id") %>%
  mutate(
      log_consumption = log(real_consumption_pc),
      runvar = dist_boundary_km * if_else(inside_mita == 1, 1, -1) # signed distance
  ) %>% 
  drop_na(log_consumption, runvar)

# 2. Main RD specification ----------------------------------------------
# Optimal bandwidth chosen automatically
rd_main <- rdrobust(y = data$log_consumption,
                    x = data$runvar,
                    covs = as.matrix(data %>% select(elevation, ruggedness)),
                    p = 1, kernel = "triangular")

summary(rd_main)

# 3. Density test for manipulation --------------------------------------
rddensity(data$runvar)$test

# 4. Conley spatial HAC --------------------------------------------------
coords <- read_csv("district_centroids.csv")       # lon, lat
data <- data %>% left_join(coords, by = "district_id")

ols <- lm(log_consumption ~ inside_mita + runvar + I(runvar^2) +
          elevation + ruggedness, data = data %>% filter(abs(runvar) < 50))

conley <- conleyreg(ols, unit = "district_id",
                    lat = "lat", lon = "lon",
                    dist = 100)                      # 100-km cutoff
conley$t

# 5. Robustness: bandwidth ±25%, donut RD -------------------------------
for(h in c(15,25,50)){
  print(rdrobust(data$log_consumption, data$runvar, h = h)$coef)
}

# Donut: drop |runvar| < 5 km
rd_donut <- rdrobust(data$log_consumption[abs(data$runvar) > 5],
                     data$runvar[abs(data$runvar) > 5])
summary(rd_donut)
```

6. Expected Results  
   Based on historical accounts of extreme mortality and subsequent institutional weakness, I expect:  
   • Log household consumption: 0.10–0.15 log‐points lower (≈10–15%) inside mita.  
   • Child height‐for‐age z-scores: −0.20 to −0.30 SD.  
   • Public goods (paved road density, school presence): 5–10 pp lower probability.  
   The effects should attenuate with distance from the boundary on the treated side, supporting a localized treatment interpretation.  

7. Validity Checklist (1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)  
   a. Running variable not manipulable: 1  
   b. Covariate continuity at cutoff: 0.8 (empirical tests pending)  
   c. No large spatial spillovers within bandwidth: 0.6  
   d. Correct inference for spatial correlation: 0.9  
   e. Robustness to bandwidths / functional forms: 1  

   Average score ≈ 0.86 → identification is strong but still depends on confirming covariate balance and limited spillovers.
